title: Area in pieces, and chance by counting
summary: Chop odd shapes into rectangles you know, draw the distributive property as one split rectangle, wrap a box in its net, then count chance from the 36 ways two dice can land and meet the next-word game hiding inside every chatbot.
materials: scissors and tape for the parallelogram slide
the two dice from your season 1 dice build
your season book and a sheet for tallies

problems.prompt: A drum loop is 4 beats long and the track repeats it 998 times. How many beats is that in all? Do it in your head.
explanation: Guess and round: 998 sits two steps below a friendly 1000.
A thousand loops would hold 4000 beats, but that counts 2 loops that never played.
Those 2 extra loops carry 8 beats, so 4000 take 8 is 3992.
problems.useAgain: when a count sits just under a friendly number, so you count with the friendly one and pay back the difference.
hints: What friendly number is 998 hiding right next to?
If you count a thousand loops instead, how many beats too many did you count?
problems.socraticHint: You just counted two loops the track never played. Where do their beats have to go at the end, and why?

variant.prompt: The same track plays a 5 beat loop 997 times. How many beats in all?

problems.prompt: An intro drum loop lost 38 beats when the editor cut it, and 47 beats were left. How many beats did the intro have before the cut?
explanation: Work backwards: the intro lost 38 beats and landed on 47, so undo the loss.
Undo a cut by adding the beats back: 47 plus 38 is 85.
Check forwards: 85 beats minus a 38 beat cut leaves 47. It closes.
problems.useAgain: when the end of a number story is known and the start is missing, so you run the story in reverse.
hints: The intro had 38 beats taken away from it. What one move undoes a take away?
Start from the beats that were left and travel back.
problems.socraticHint: If cutting 38 beats carried the intro down to 47, what single move carries it home again?

variant.prompt: A second loop lost 26 beats to a cut and 48 beats were left. How many beats did it have before the cut?

problems.prompt: Three drum tracks: one is 19 bars of 21 beats, one is 20 bars of 20 beats, one is 18 bars of 22 beats. Without working all three out fully, which track holds the most beats?
explanation: Guess and round: 20 bars of 20 beats is the easy anchor, 400 beats.
19 bars of 21 is 19 bars of 20 plus one spare beat in each bar: 380 plus 19 is 399.
18 bars of 22 is 18 bars of 20 plus two spare beats in each bar: 360 plus 36 is 396.
So 400 wins: an evener split of the same total makes the bigger product.
problems.useAgain: when products need comparing and each one sits a small repair away from an easy anchor.
hints: Find the track you can total instantly and use it as the measuring stick.
Turn each other track into the anchor plus or minus a small repair.
problems.socraticHint: In all three tracks the bars and the beats add up to 40. Why does trading one up and the other down not leave the product alone?

variant.prompt: Same job, bigger tracks: 29 bars of 31 beats, 28 bars of 32 beats, or 30 bars of 30 beats. Which holds the most beats?

problems.prompt: A metronome rings a bell every 25 beats: beat 300, beat 325, beat 350 and on. Which is the first bell past beat 380?
explanation: Find the rule: every bell in a count by 25s lands on a number ending in 00, 25, 50 or 75.
Near beat 380 the candidates are 375 and 400, and 375 rings too early.
So the first bell past beat 380 rings on beat 400.
problems.useAgain: when a skip count leaves a fingerprint in its endings, so you jump straight to the landing spots near your target.
hints: What do the last two digits of every bell in a count by 25s look like?
List the bells on either side of beat 380.
problems.socraticHint: Why can a bell every 25 beats never ring on a beat number ending in 80?

variant.prompt: The same metronome rings every 25 beats from beat 300. Which is the first bell past beat 430?

problem.prompt: A big cube is built from 27 small cubes, 3 by 3 by 3. You dip the whole big cube in paint and let it dry. When you take it apart, how many of the 27 small cubes have paint on exactly two of their faces? Build it in your head layer by layer, or sketch the three layers on graph paper before you answer.
explanation: Count the hidden ones: sort the small cubes by where they live, not one by one.

A corner cube shows three faces to the paint, a cube in the middle of a flat side shows one, and the very middle cube shows none. Exactly two painted faces belongs to the cubes that live along an edge but not at a corner.
Each edge of the big cube holds 3 small cubes: a corner, a middle, a corner. So each edge gives exactly one two-face cube.
A cube has 12 edges, so 12 small cubes wear paint on exactly two faces.
Check the census: 8 corners, 12 edge middles, 6 face middles, 1 hidden heart. 8 + 12 + 6 + 1 is 27, everyone counted.
problem.useAgain: when a big shape is built from small pieces and the pieces sort into kinds by where they sit.
hints: Where does a small cube have to live to touch the paint on exactly two sides: a corner, along an edge, the middle of a flat face, or deep inside?
Count how many spots of that kind the whole big cube has.
problem.socraticHint: What is different about the neighbourhood of a corner cube, an edge cube and a face cube?

variant.prompt: The same painted 3 by 3 by 3 cube is taken apart. How many of the 27 small cubes have paint on exactly one face? Sketch the three layers on graph paper before you answer.

problems.prompt: A garage floor is an L-shape made of a 9 by 6 rectangle and a 5 by 4 rectangle that overlap in a 3 by 4 shared corner. What is the true floor area, in square units?
explanation: Area in pieces: split the L-shape into a 9 by 6 rectangle and a 5 by 4 rectangle, which cover 54 and 20 square units.
Adding 54 and 20 double-counts the 3 by 4 corner both rectangles share, which is 12 square units.
Subtract that shared corner once: 54 plus 20 minus 12 is 62.
Whenever two pieces overlap, add the pieces then subtract the overlap exactly once.
problems.useAgain: when two pieces of a shape overlap and adding their areas would count the shared part twice.
hints: Find the area of each of the two rectangles first, before combining them.
The two rectangles share a corner. Adding both areas counts that shared corner twice.
problems.socraticHint: If two pieces share some ground, does simply adding their areas count that ground once or twice?

variant.prompt: A patio floor is an L-shape made of a 7 by 5 rectangle and a 4 by 6 rectangle that overlap in a 2 by 5 shared corner. What is the true floor area, in square units?

problems.prompt: A right triangle on graph paper has one leg 6 squares long and the other leg 8 squares long, meeting at the square corner. What is its area, in grid squares?
explanation: Area in pieces: every right triangle is half of a rectangle.
Draw the 6 by 8 rectangle whose two sides are the triangle's legs: 48 squares.
The diagonal cuts that rectangle into two matching triangles, so yours holds half of 48, which is 24.
problems.useAgain: when a triangle has a square corner, so you box it into a rectangle and take half.
hints: Draw the full rectangle that the two legs belong to.
The diagonal splits that rectangle into two pieces. Compare them.
problems.socraticHint: How do you know the diagonal splits the rectangle into two exactly equal pieces?

variant.prompt: A right triangle on graph paper has legs 5 squares and 6 squares meeting at the square corner. What is its area, in grid squares?

problems.prompt: A parallelogram on graph paper leans like a pushed-over rectangle: its bottom side is 7 squares long and its height straight up is 4 squares. Draw it, cut the leaning triangle off one end with scissors, and slide that piece to the other end. What is the parallelogram's area, in grid squares?
explanation: Area in pieces: the slide turns the leaning shape into a rectangle without gaining or losing a single square.
The triangle you cut from one end fits exactly into the hole at the other end, leaving a 7 by 4 rectangle.
7 x 4 is 28, so the parallelogram held 28 squares all along.
problems.useAgain: when a shape can be cut and slid into a rectangle, because moving a piece never changes the total area.
hints: Cut straight up from a bottom corner and look at the triangle that comes off.
Where does that triangle fit on the other end, and what shape is left behind?
problems.socraticHint: Why does sliding a cut piece somewhere else leave the total area exactly the same?

variant.prompt: A parallelogram leans like a pushed-over rectangle: bottom side 9 squares, height straight up 3 squares. Cut and slide the leaning end. What is its area, in grid squares?

problems.prompt: One rectangle, 6 squares tall and 14 squares wide, is split by one straight line into a 6 by 10 part and a 6 by 4 part. Which expression counts its area?
explanation: Area in pieces: the split line cuts one big rectangle into two smaller ones, and the big area is the two small areas added.
The left piece holds 6 x 10, which is 60. The right piece holds 6 x 4, which is 24.
So the whole is 6 x 10 plus 6 x 4, which is 84, and 6 x 14 counted in one go agrees.
You just drew the distributive property: 6 x 14 is 6 x (10 plus 4), and the picture shows why the 6 must multiply both parts.
problems.useAgain: when a hard multiplication splits into two easy ones because the rectangle splits into two easy rectangles.
hints: Find the area of each of the two pieces on its own.
How do the two piece areas combine into the whole rectangle's area?
problems.socraticHint: The 14 got split into 10 and 4. Why does the 6 have to multiply both parts instead of just one of them?

variant.prompt: One rectangle, 5 squares tall and 17 squares wide, is split by one line into a 5 by 10 part and a 5 by 7 part. Which expression counts its area?

problems.prompt:
Beatrix combined 9 x 4 plus 9 x 6 in one move.
Line 1: Both products share a 9, so picture two rectangles that are both 9 tall.
Line 2: Stand them side by side: the glued rectangle is 9 tall and 4 + 6 wide, which is 10 wide.
Line 3: The glued rectangle's area is 9 x 10.
Line 4: 9 x 10 is 80.
Which line is wrong?
explanation: Lines 1 through 3 are correct: the two rectangles glue into one 9 by 10 rectangle.
Line 4 is wrong: 9 times 10 is 90, not 80.
Area in pieces, run in reverse: gluing along the shared side turns two multiplications into one.
But the final multiplication still has to be done correctly.
9 x 4 plus 9 x 6 is really 90.
problems.useAgain: when two products are correctly glued into one rectangle but the final multiplication still needs its own check.
hints: Do not assume any line is correct just because the ones before it look fine. Recompute each line yourself, including which number the two products actually share.
Area in pieces: gluing rectangles works only when you find the side they truly share, and the final multiplication still has to be done right.
problems.socraticHint: Do the two products actually share the number this working picked out as their common side?

variant.prompt:
Callum combined 6 x 11 plus 6 x 9 in one move.
Line 1: Both products share an 11, so picture two rectangles that are both 11 tall.
Line 2: Stand them side by side: the glued rectangle is 11 tall and 6 + 9 wide, which is 15 wide.
Line 3: The glued rectangle's area is 11 x 15.
Line 4: 11 x 15 is 165.
Which line is wrong?

problems.prompt: You are drawing the net for a closed box on graph paper. The box is 4 long, 3 wide and 2 tall. Five faces are drawn so far: 4 by 3, 4 by 3, 4 by 2, 4 by 2 and 3 by 2. Which face is missing?
explanation: Fold it in your head: a closed box has six faces, and they come in matching pairs, top with bottom, front with back, left with right.
The 4 by 3 pair is complete, and so is the 4 by 2 pair.
The 3 by 2 face stands alone, so the missing face is its twin: another 3 by 2.
problems.useAgain: when a box's faces need checking, because the three matching pairs tell you exactly what a net must contain.
hints: Sort the five drawn faces into pairs of matching twins.
Which face is standing alone without its twin?
problems.socraticHint: Why do a box's faces always come in equal pairs?

variant.prompt: The same job for a box 5 long, 3 wide and 2 tall. Drawn so far: 5 by 2, 5 by 2, 5 by 3, 3 by 2 and 3 by 2. Which face is missing?

problems.prompt: Now wrap that box: 4 long, 3 wide, 2 tall. Using its net, add up all six faces. How many grid squares of paper cover the whole box, with no overlaps?
explanation: Fold it in your head: the net lays all six faces flat where you can count them.
The three different face sizes are 4 x 3 which is 12, 4 x 2 which is 8, and 3 x 2 which is 6.
Each size comes as a pair, so the total is 2 x 12 plus 2 x 8 plus 2 x 6.
24 plus 16 plus 12 is 52 grid squares. That number is the box's surface area.
problems.useAgain: when a box needs wrapping or painting, so you total all six faces from its net instead of guessing.
hints: Work out the three different face sizes first: length by width, length by height, width by height.
Each of the three sizes appears exactly twice on a closed box.
problems.socraticHint: Where does each face's twin sit on the box, and why can no face go without one?

variant.prompt: Wrap a box 5 long, 2 wide and 2 tall. How many grid squares cover all six faces, with no overlaps?

steps.title: Four ways to fold it flat, and the sum every table agrees on

problems.prompt: A plus-sign shape is made of 5 equal squares (shown shaded): one center square with one square attached on each of its four sides. How many lines of symmetry does it have?
explanation: A line of symmetry folds the shape exactly onto itself, with no square left uncovered or overhanging.
This plus-sign folds perfectly along its vertical middle, its horizontal middle, and both diagonals through the center.
That is 4 different lines of symmetry.
problems.useAgain: when counting a shape's lines of symmetry, by checking every line that would fold one half exactly onto the other.
hints: Try folding the shape along its vertical middle, its horizontal middle, and each diagonal. Which folds match up exactly?
A true line of symmetry leaves no square sticking out on either side.
problems.socraticHint: If you folded this shape along one of its diagonals, would every square land exactly on top of another square?

figure.alt: A plus-sign made of five equal squares in a 3 by 3 grid: the center square, plus one square directly above, below, left and right of it.

variant.prompt: A solid rectangle shape is made of 2 rows and 4 columns of equal squares (8 squares total, not a square overall). How many lines of symmetry does it have?

problems.prompt: Point (2, 5) is reflected across the horizontal line y = 1. What is the y-coordinate of its new position?
explanation: The point sits 4 units above the mirror line, since 5 minus 1 is 4.
The reflection lands that same 4 units below the mirror: 1 minus 4 is -3.
The x-coordinate never changes in a reflection across a horizontal line.
problems.useAgain: when a point reflects across a horizontal line that is not the x-axis, by measuring its distance from the mirror.
hints: How far above the line y = 1 does the point sit?
The reflection lands that same distance on the other side of the line.
problems.socraticHint: Does reflecting a point across a horizontal line ever change how far left or right it sits?

variant.prompt: Point (2, -2) is reflected across the horizontal line y = 3. What is the y-coordinate of its new position?

problems.prompt: Using the two-dice sum table (36 equally likely rolls), what is the probability, as a fraction in lowest terms, that the sum is a multiple of 3?
explanation: Sums that are multiples of 3 are 3, 6, 9 and 12, made in 2, 5, 4 and 1 ways.
2 plus 5 plus 4 plus 1 is 12 ways out of 36.
12 out of 36 simplifies to 1/3.
problems.useAgain: when a probability question groups together several sums at once by a shared rule, like being a multiple of 3.
hints: Which sums from 2 to 12 are multiples of 3?
Add up the ways for each of those sums before dividing by 36.
problems.socraticHint: Does grouping several sums together mean adding their individual ways, or multiplying them?

variant.prompt: Using the same two-dice sum table, what is the probability, as a fraction in lowest terms, that the sum is even?

problems.prompt: Using the same two-dice sum table, how many ways can each of the least likely sums, 2 or 12, be made?
explanation: A sum of 2 can only come from 1 and 1, and a sum of 12 can only come from 6 and 6.
Both of those sums have exactly 1 way to be made, the fewest of any sum on the table.
problems.useAgain: when the least or most likely sum on a two-dice table needs identifying by comparing how many ways each one has.
hints: Which two numbers on the dice can make a sum of 2? Is there more than one pair?
The same question for a sum of 12.
problems.socraticHint: Why might the extreme sums, 2 and 12, always end up with the fewest ways among all the sums?

variant.prompt: Using the same two-dice sum table, how many ways can the most likely sum, 7, be made?

figure.alt: White to move. A white queen on d1 faces an undefended black knight on d5 and a black rook on g4 that a pawn on h5 defends.

problems.prompt: White to move. One black piece is undefended and one is defended. Which move wins material safely?
explanation: The rook on g4 is guarded by black's own pawn on h5, so trading your queen for it loses material.
The knight on d5 has no defender at all.
Qxd5 wins the knight for free.
problems.useAgain: when more than one enemy piece looks capturable, so check who defends what before you choose.
hints: For each piece you could capture, ask who else is watching that square.
Pick the capture where nothing can take your piece back.
problems.socraticHint: Which of these two captures would black be happy to let you make?

variant.prompt: White to move. One black piece is undefended and one is defended. Which move wins material safely?

figure.alt: White to move. A white rook on a1 faces an undefended black bishop on a6 and a black knight on c1 that a pawn defends.
White to move. Black's king on a8 is boxed in by pawns on a7 and b7, with a white rook on h1.

problems.prompt: White to move. Which move gives checkmate?
explanation: Black's king on a8 has only its own pawns for neighbours.
Rh8 slides all the way across the open back rank to check it.
No pawn or piece can stop the rook, so it is mate.
problems.useAgain: when a king is boxed in by its own pawns and the back rank is open.
hints: Which row is completely open between your rook and the black king?
Slide the rook all the way across that row.
problems.socraticHint: Could black's pawns ever move backward to block this rook?

variant.prompt: White to move. Which move gives checkmate?

figure.alt: White to move. Black's king on h8 is boxed in by pawns on g7 and h7, with a white rook on a1.
White to move. A white knight on d3 faces a black queen on b7 and a black rook on d7.

problems.prompt: White to move. Which move attacks the black queen and rook at once?
explanation: A knight jumping to c5 attacks both b7 and d7 at the same time.
Black's queen and rook sit on exactly those two squares.
Black can only save one of them.
problems.useAgain: when a single knight jump lands on a square that touches two valuable pieces.
hints: Look for a knight square that touches two black pieces worth more than a knight.
Check both b7 and d7 from that square.
problems.socraticHint: Which of the two pieces would black choose to save?

variant.prompt: White to move. Which move attacks two black rooks at once?

figure.alt: White to move. A white knight on g3 faces two undefended black rooks on d6 and f6.
Black to move. Black's king sits alone on h8, boxed in by a white king on f6 and a white queen on f7.

problems.prompt: It is black's move. The king has no square to go to. Is this checkmate, stalemate, or does black have another legal move?
explanation: The black king on h8 cannot move to g8, g7 or h7, because the white queen and king cover all three.
The white queen does not actually attack h8 itself, so the king is not in check.
No legal move and no check together mean the game is a draw by stalemate.
problems.useAgain: when a king has no square to move to but is not actually in check.
hints: First check every square next to the king. Can it move anywhere?
Now check the king's own square. Is it actually under attack right now?
problems.socraticHint: Does having no moves always mean the same thing as being checkmated?

variant.prompt: It is black's move. The king has no square to go to. Is this checkmate, stalemate, or does black have another legal move?

figure.alt: Black to move. Black's king sits alone on h8, boxed in by a white king on g6 and a white queen on h7.

steps.title: Two table experiments before the puzzles
steps.body:
Two quick experiments feed the puzzle set, so run them first, tally sheets out.

Experiment one: fetch the two dice from your season 1 dice build. Roll the pair 50 times. Keep two tallies as you go: one mark every time the total is 7, and one mark every time both dice show the same face. Do not judge anything yet. Just roll and tally.

Experiment two: open your season book to any full page. Pick a common little word on that page, like the, or a, or she. Read the page with a pencil, and every time your word appears, tally which word comes right after it. By the bottom of the page you own a tally table: your word, then each follower with its count.

Keep both sheets beside you. The puzzle set will tell you what counting promises, your sheets will tell you what the world actually did, and the gap between those two is this week's whole idea.

steps.title: Chance is counting, and the next word

problems.prompt: Roll two dice, one red and one blue. The red die can land 6 ways, and for each of those the blue die can land 6 ways. How many different ways can the pair land?
explanation: Choices multiply: when one choice stacks on another, multiply the ways.
Each of the red die's 6 faces pairs up with each of the blue die's 6 faces.
6 x 6 is 36 ways. You could list them all in a 6 by 6 grid on graph paper, red faces down the side, blue faces along the top, one square per way.
problems.useAgain: when choices stack one after another and you want the count of all the combinations.
hints: Fix the red die on one face for a moment. How many things can the blue die still do?
That same count happens once for every face the red die can show.
problems.socraticHint: Why is the count of pairs a multiplication, and not 6 plus 6?

variant.prompt: Roll one die and flip one coin. How many different ways can the pair land?

problems.prompt: Out of the 36 ways two dice can land, how many ways make the total 7?
explanation: Count the ways: chance begins with counting the ways you want against all the ways there are.
Walk the red die through its faces: red 1 needs blue 6, red 2 needs blue 5, red 3 needs blue 4, red 4 needs blue 3, red 5 needs blue 2, red 6 needs blue 1.
Every red face has exactly one blue partner, so 6 ways make 7.
That is why 7 is the king of totals: its chance is 6 out of 36, which is 1 out of 6, more than any other total gets.
problems.useAgain: when every outcome is equally likely, so a chance is just the wanted ways counted against all the ways.
hints: Go one red face at a time: if the red die shows 1, what must the blue die show?
Check every red face in turn: does each one have a blue partner that works?
problems.socraticHint: The total 12 gets only one way. What is it about 7 that hands it so many?

variant.prompt: Out of the 36 ways two dice can land, how many ways make the total 4?

problems.prompt: True or false: rolling a total of 2 is exactly as likely as rolling a total of 12.
explanation: Count the ways: a total of 2 needs red 1 and blue 1, one single way out of 36.
A total of 12 needs red 6 and blue 6, also one single way.
One way each, so the two totals are exactly equally likely, even though 2 feels tiny and 12 feels grand. The counting does not care how a number feels.
problems.useAgain: when two events need comparing and counting their ways settles it without any feelings.
hints: List every pair of faces that makes a total of 2.
Now list every pair that makes 12, and compare the lengths of your two lists.
problems.socraticHint: What exactly would a total need more of, to be more likely than another total?

variant.prompt: True or false: rolling a total of 6 is exactly as likely as rolling a total of 7.

problems.prompt: The counting says the chance of a total of 7 is 6 out of 36, which is 1 out of 6. If you roll the pair 36 times, about how many sevens does the long run promise?
explanation: The long run: a chance of 1 out of 6 means about one seven in every six rolls, once the rolls pile up.
36 rolls hold six groups of six rolls, so the promise is about 6 sevens.
About is the honest word. Your actual 36 rolls might give 4 sevens or 9: chance is wobbly in a short run and only calms down when the run gets long.
problems.useAgain: when a chance needs turning into an expected count, so you take that fraction of the number of tries.
hints: A chance of one in six means one seven for about every how many rolls?
How many groups of that size fit into 36 rolls?
problems.socraticHint: A real batch of 36 rolls might land a few sevens above or below the promise. What is the promise actually about, if not any single batch?

variant.prompt: Doubles have a chance of 6 out of 36, which is 1 out of 6. If you roll the pair 60 times, about how many doubles does the long run promise?

problems.prompt: A 50 roll tally shows 12 sevens, but the counting only promised about 8. Which is the honest reading?
options: Fifty rolls is still a short run, and short runs wobble
Sevens are secretly luckier than the counting says
explanation: The long run: the promise is an average over a huge number of rolls, not a guarantee for any particular 50.
In 50 rolls, drifting a few above or below the promised 8 is completely ordinary.
The dice also have no memory: no roll owes you anything, and no streak changes the next roll.
Roll a few hundred more times and the sevens fraction will drift toward 1 out of 6 on its own. Set your own 50 roll sheet next to this and see which side of the promise your wobble landed on.
problems.useAgain: when a real tally disagrees a little with the counted chance and you must decide whether anything is actually wrong.
hints: Ask what the counted chance actually promises, and over how many rolls.
How far off would a tally need to be, and for how long, before the dice themselves became the best suspect?
problems.socraticHint: If you rolled 5000 times and sevens still came up a quarter of the time, would your answer change? What separates ordinary wobble from a real signal?

variant.prompt: A 50 roll tally shows only 4 sevens, but the counting promised about 8. Which is the honest reading?
options: Short runs wobble, and fifty rolls is still a short run
The dice remember the drought and now owe extra sevens

problems.prompt: Suppose a next-word tally from one page of a book came out like this. After the word the: sea 5 times, boat 2 times, morning 1 time. You cover the page and play. Which word is the best guess to come after the?
explanation: Next-word guessing: the game backs the follower with the biggest tally.
Sea followed the 5 times out of 8, more than boat and morning put together.
Best guess does not mean sure: 3 times out of 8 the page went another way, so a good guesser expects to lose sometimes and backs sea anyway.
Every chatbot plays exactly this game, with a tally built from oceans of pages instead of one.
problems.useAgain: when a guess must come from counts, so you back the option the tally has seen most.
hints: The tally is the whole game: which follower did the page use most often?
Compare each count against the others before you commit.
problems.socraticHint: Can a guess be the best possible one and still turn out wrong almost half the time?

variant.prompt: Same game, new tally. After the word a, the counts are: wave 1 time, ship 4 times, day 2 times. Which word is the best guess to come after a?

problems.prompt: Your next-word tally came from one page. A chatbot's tally comes from more pages than you could read in a thousand lifetimes. Why does its next-word game play so much better than yours?
options: It understands the story the way a person does
Its tally has seen far more examples than yours
explanation: Data teaches the machine: the smart part came from the examples, exactly like your robot in week 6.

That tally met the word the 8 times, so a perfectly good follower may never have shown up at all. A tally built from oceans of pages has met the in millions of sentences, in every mood a sentence can have.
More examples make steadier counts and better guesses, the same way your dice tally calms down as the run gets long.
And it can still be wrong: a best guess from counts is a guess, whoever holds the tally.
problems.useAgain: when a guesser seems clever and you ask what examples its guesses were built from.
hints: Think back to week 6: where did your robot's smartness actually come from?
Compare how many times each tally has ever met the word the.
problems.socraticHint: If you tallied ten more pages tonight, what would happen to your game? What does that say about where the machine's advantage lives?

variant.prompt: Your friend tallied one paragraph. You tallied the whole page. Whose next-word game should play better, and why?
options: Yours, because your tally has seen more examples
Your friend's, because the paragraph is fresher
Both exactly the same, tallies are tallies

steps.title: Explain it in writing
steps.prompt: Write, in your own words, why 6 x 14 and 6 x 10 plus 6 x 4 must always land on the same number, and draw the split rectangle that proves it. Then chop one more shape: if your free build plan has a flat part with an odd footprint, chop that shape into easy pieces on graph paper and find its area. If it does not, go back to the shelf plank from the first skills problem and cut it a third way, one straight cut from top to bottom instead of side to side, and show that this count lands on 34 too.

steps.title: Explain it out loud
steps.prompt: Record yourself teaching the next-word game to a grown-up: how your tally played it on one page of your season book, why the biggest count makes the best guess, why the best guess still loses sometimes, and what a chatbot's tally has that yours does not.
